name: Elena Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee jumbo operator at an underground zinc mine. A jumbo is a drill rig with two long arms, and we drill the face of the tunnel so the charge-up crew can blast it. I've been underground a bit over a year. Before that I ran the office for my parents' small earthmoving business for sixteen years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you go underground at forty-two?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The family business slowed down when the big contractors started winning all the council work, and my parents needed to pay themselves less. Somebody had to bring in a proper wage. I still do their books on Sunday nights with an AI assistant that sorts the receipts, which my dad thinks is witchcraft. Underground, I'm the slowest on the jumbo, my holes wander, but Tomas, the old operator who trains me, says I learn quicker than the young ones because I actually read the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be a bit let down, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, the market had its say. People tried it, it didn't deliver enough, so they moved on. I'd mention it after Mass to the men who were all worked up about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd hoped some of this would help the family business compete with the big contractors. But for my job, it's good, I'd get time to become a proper jumbo operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep training on the jumbo and try for my full ticket by next winter. I'd keep using AI for my parents' books and quoting, because it already saves us hours. We'd keep building the savings, about three months now, toward six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day, even if it's a plateau. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sorting receipts, drafting quotes for my dad's excavator jobs, checking the safety rules for the jumbo when I'm not sure. Last month it caught a double payment to a fuel supplier that we'd missed for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if the AI hype faded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say he told me so, but he'd keep using the quotes it writes. Mum doesn't care either way as long as Lucia gets to her dancing.

S0.say: I'd say the market had its say: people tried it, it didn't deliver enough, so they moved on. I'd mention it after Mass to the men who were worked up about robots.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed because I hoped AI would help the family business compete. For my own job it's good; I'd get time to become a proper jumbo operator.
S0.do: Keeps training on the jumbo and aims for her full ticket by next winter. Keeps using AI for her parents' books and quotes, and builds savings from three months toward six.
S0.quote: Last month it caught a double payment to a fuel supplier that we'd missed for a year.
S0.fieldNote: Elena is traditional in faith and family but enthusiastic about technology, which she already uses to run her parents' business books. She'd be mildly disappointed by a plateau. Her mine job is about bringing in a steady wage for the wider family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd actually like, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. Business will always look for a better way, and that's fine. But I'd say families and churches need to look after the ones who struggle with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. Remote drilling from the surface is already happening at some mines, and I'm comfortable with screens. And the family business could use the same tools to compete with the big contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine this year to get me on the remote drilling trial and do the training as soon as it's offered. I'd help my dad buy a used excavator with GPS guidance, maybe thirty thousand, so he can bid on jobs he's losing now. I'd keep saving, but I'd take the risk on the excavator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your dad buy an excavator. Where would that money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part from the business savings, part a loan in the business's name, and maybe a little from us. Marco wouldn't love that, he's more careful than me. We'd argue, then I'd show him the numbers and he'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas. He's sixty-one and he can read a rock face like a book, but he won't touch a tablet. I'd want the mine to keep him on as a trainer, because the machines will still need someone who knows where the ground's bad.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to work and learn, and business looking for a better way is fine. Families and churches should look after those who struggle.
S1.think: I think I'd do well because remote drilling is already happening and I'm comfortable with screens. The family business could use the same tools to compete.
S1.do: Asks to join the remote drilling trial this year and trains as soon as it's offered. Helps her father buy a used GPS-guided excavator for about thirty thousand, partly on a business loan.
S1.quote: We'd argue, then I'd show him the numbers and he'd agree.
S1.fieldNote: Elena sees steady change as a chance at both her mine job and her family's business. She's comfortable taking a measured financial risk, while her husband is the careful one. She wants the mine to keep her older trainer on for his ground knowledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people shouldn't wait for the government to save them. Families, parishes and local businesses need to pull together, and fast. I'd still back help for those who've got nothing, but as a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried for the first time. If AGI does everything by 2028, remote drilling goes too, and the big contractors would have robot fleets that crush my dad's business. Being good with technology doesn't help much when the technology doesn't need you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop the excavator plan and keep every dollar, because it'd be the wrong machine by then. I'd use AI to find whatever small, local work robots won't get to first, like jobs on tight private blocks the big fleets won't bother with. And we'd think twice about sending Gianni to the Catholic boarding school we'd been saving for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My mind's racing for answers, which is better than freezing, but my stomach is in knots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no time to build anything. You'd be spending your savings to stand still. With five or ten, I could build the family business into something that rides the change instead of getting run over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd reconsider boarding school for Gianni. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. He's fourteen and his cousins go there. I'd tell him the money might need to keep the roof over us, and that family comes before a school badge.

S2.say: I'd say people shouldn't wait for government to save them: families, parishes and local businesses should pull together fast, with help for those with nothing as a bridge.
S2.think: I think I'd be worried for the first time, because remote drilling goes too and robot fleets would crush my dad's business. Being good with technology doesn't help when it doesn't need you.
S2.do: Drops the excavator plan and keeps every dollar. Uses AI to hunt for small local jobs the big robot fleets would skip, and reconsiders the boarding school they'd been saving for.
S2.feel: Anxious, her mind racing for answers and her stomach in knots.
S2.quote: Being good with technology doesn't help much when the technology doesn't need you.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the first picture that shakes Elena; her adaptability no longer buys her a place. She shifts from investing to protecting cash and hunting for niches. The boarding school decision shows how quickly it would reach her family plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, now I'm thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready if people stop complaining and start working on it. Learn the tools, change how your business runs. I'd tell the women at church to make sure their kids learn practical skills as well as screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me and Dad a window. I'd get onto remote drilling, earn well, and we'd turn the family business into a small, modern operation that does the jobs the big fleets don't want. By 2031 I don't know if it survives, but it's a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote drilling course in the first year and push my income up. With Dad, I'd buy the GPS excavator after all, but only once we'd seen two or three other small firms make it pay. I'd use AI every day to run the quoting and scheduling so the business stays lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a working mood. Like the night before a big shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for other small firms to make it pay. Is that different from how you'd act in the slow picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. When there's less time, a wrong bet hurts more. So I'd still move early, just not first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco, your husband? Where is he in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco works for the council parks crew, and they'll probably keep people longer than the mine. His wage is the steady one, mine is the gamble. That's why I can take a few risks.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop complaining and start working: learn the tools, change how your business runs, and teach kids practical skills too.
S3.think: I think five years gives my father and me a window to modernise the family business while I earn well on remote drilling. It may not survive past 2031, but it's a real chance.
S3.do: Takes the remote drilling course in the first year to lift her income. Buys the GPS excavator with her father only after seeing other small firms make it pay, and runs quoting and scheduling with AI.
S3.feel: Uneasy but ready to work, like the night before a big shift.
S3.quote: His wage is the steady one, mine is the gamble.
S3.fieldNote: Five years reopens Elena's plan for the family business, but she becomes more cautious about timing. Her husband's council job is what lets her take risks. She frames her preparation as work, in line with her traditional views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a real plan's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and there's no excuse for not using it. Work hard, learn, look after your family. That's what my nonna would've said, and she ran a shop through a war.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. Ten years is enough to build Dad's business into something modern, get the kids through school and pay down a big chunk of the mortgage. By the time AGI arrives I'd want to be the one owning the robot, not the one replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the jumbo and move to remote drilling over the first couple of years. With Dad, we'd plan to modernise the business in stages, one machine every few years, with AI running the paperwork. And I'd start a small share portfolio, a few hundred a month, in companies building the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, mostly, with some respect for how big it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to own the robot. What does that look like for a family business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of self-driving excavators doing the boring trenching while Dad and I deal with customers and the tricky jobs. People still want to shake a hand before someone digs up their yard. That's what I'm betting on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My kids. Gianni and Lucia will grow up into a world I can't picture. I'd want them to have faith, a trade and some of that cheek my nonna had.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long runway with no excuse not to use it: work hard, learn and look after your family, like my nonna did running a shop through a war.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine, with time to modernise the family business, get the kids through school and pay down the mortgage. When AGI arrives I want to own the robot, not be replaced by it.
S4.do: Moves from the jumbo into remote drilling over the first couple of years. Plans to modernise the family business one machine at a time with AI handling paperwork, and invests a few hundred a month in shares.
S4.feel: Calm and excited, with respect for how big the change is.
S4.quote: I'd want to be the one owning the robot, not the one replaced by it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Elena's adaptability and business instincts work fully. She bets on people wanting to shake a hand before work starts on their land. Her remaining worry is her children's future, which she ties to faith and a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is help for small family businesses to get the new machines, like low-interest loans, rather than all of it going to the big contractors. And keeping the older people like Tomas on as trainers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of us would get through this because of our church and our families, not because of any program. People forget that when they write the plans.

headlineQuote: People still want to shake a hand before someone digs up their yard.
portrait: Elena Rossi is 43, a trainee jumbo operator at an underground zinc mine who ran the office of her parents' earthmoving business for sixteen years. She's traditional, church-going and free-market, and also an everyday AI user who does her parents' books with an AI assistant. She sees Steady Disruption as an opening for remote drilling and for modernising the family business. Fast AGI shakes her because her skills no longer buy a place, but with five or ten years she plans to own the machines rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no time to build anything and robot fleets would crush her father's business.
whatWouldHelp: Low-interest loans and other help for small family businesses to buy new machines, and keeping older workers on as trainers.
